rationale: A wins because it stays closer to the supplied facts while still finding real tension. Its "Going plans the trip. You still book it yourself. That gap is the story." is a clean reporter test; B's "Expedia, Kayak, and Hopper have bolted AI planners onto their products" drags in unsupplied competitor facts and makes the founder defend your homework. B has usable bones, but A is the set I would let near a journalist after proof collection.
gaps_in_A: "most trip-planning tools start with a destination or a date" is plausible, but it is still an outside category claim. Prove it or soften it before pitching.
"A tech business reporter covering SaaS subscription models" is slightly off-category. Going is a consumer subscription/membership business, not SaaS; sloppy beat labeling gets pitches deleted.
"a deal-alert brand's long reinvention" may be right, but the update only gives former name plus this launch. It needs dates, prior product moves, and rebrand context before it earns "long."
gaps_in_B: "Expedia, Kayak, and Hopper have bolted AI planners onto their products" is not in the supplied facts. That is exactly the kind of confident outside claim that burns trust.
"differs from everyone else already building the same feature" overclaims the competitive landscape before doing the reporting. The proof section admits the angle has not earned its own premise.
"AI will handle your whole trip end-to-end" narratives circulating in travel tech" is a strawman until current coverage proves it exists. Do not build a contrarian angle on a vibe.
The product-design angle asks for "any usage data" but misses the more useful proof: a named paid member who went from alert to itinerary to booking. Without that human, this is still a spec sheet.
